newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian cosmonaut Tsibliyev faces tough questions.
newsitem.headline: Russian cosmonaut Tsibliyev faces tough questions.

text.p: Vasily Tsibliyev, the commander of the troubled Mir space station who landed safely back on Earth on Thursday, has spent his life flirting with danger as an air force pilot and cosmonaut.
But the 43-year-old Tsibliyev had never been through anything quite as tough as the six-month mission he has just completed in charge on the orbiting Mir station.

Problems that jinxed the mission included a collision while he was at the controls, power and oxygen supply failures, a fire and his own stress-induced heart condition after the crash, which was the worst accident in Mir's 11-year history.

In a touching gesture, Tsibliyev told the three crew members remaining on Mir he hoped to take the bad luck with him. "I hope that everything bad that we've had will leave with us," Tsibliyev said as he prepared to leave the crippled station.
Back on Earth, he smiled broadly as he emerged from the Soyuz capsule. "What other feelings could we have, just happy to be back," he said.
But Tsibliyev is sure to face some tough questions back on Earth to explain what went wrong.
He will also have to handle some bad personal news that his mother kept from him while he was in space -- his stepfather died of a heart attack five months ago.

Tsibliyev was born in Orekhovka in Ukraine and was brought up in poverty. He trained to be a pilot and flew Soviet MiG-21 fighter jets from bases in East Germnay and Moldova after qualifying from the Kharkiv aviation school.
He got the idea of becoming a cosmonaut after Yuri Gagarin became the first man in space in 1961.
Tsibliyev's latest mission quickly ran into trouble after he blasted off from Earth on February 10 and docked on February 12 for his second stay on Mir.

A fire broke out when the cosmonauts tried to change a filter on February 23 and the crew had to put on gas masks because of fumes that irritated their throats. The blaze was extinguished after seven minutes.
On March 6, a Progress cargo craft failed to dock with Mir and was dumped. The next day an oxygen supply generator failed, forcing the crew to use backup chemical system and put on gas masks again.
Almost a month later, Mir developed a leak in its cooling system which briefly knocked out a device used to maintain breathable air on board.
Worse was to come.
Another Progress hit Mir during a practice docking, puncturing the Spektr module attached to the space station, damaging a solar battery and forcing the crew to cut cables to three others.
In the stressful time that followed, one of the crew mistakenly pulled out a vital computer cable on July 17, prompting a power failure which was rectified within 24 hours.
Tsbiliyev also developed an irregular heartbeat, diagnosed as arrhythmia. He was put on sedatives and heart pills and Mission Control put plans to fix the Spektr on hold.
"Naturally the internal anxiety, emotional stress and the sense of responsibility which he is suffering are all having an effect on him," one Mission Control official said at the time.
Tsibliyev tried to take it all in his stride. "We have been through some very dark times, but we are over them," he said while still on Mir.
His 64-year-old mother spent the mission praying her son would come back alive.

His wife, Larisa, said her husband's training would pull him through. And if that did not work, he could count on the plastic bunny lucky charm his daughter gave him: "It's not pretty. But it always works."
